highlights: Europe remains a critical energy outlet

frictionVectors.title: EU ENERGY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over gas production and export infrastructure, but European demand, pricing, and diversification efforts constrain its bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: SAHARA SECURITY NETWORKS
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger pressures Algeria to expand border security while resisting deeper foreign military involvement in the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-BACKED INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain central to transport and energy infrastructure, creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence risks.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL DECLINE
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and dependence on foreign operators limit Angola's effective control over production, while new investment is needed to sustain state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's expansion improves Benin's leverage, but trade remains exposed to Nigerian policy shifts and regional transport bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL MILITANT SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist activity from Burkina Faso and Niger threatens northern communities and may force greater reliance on external security assistance.

highlights: Diversification is now a strategic necessity

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND MARKET EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial negotiating power over diamond extraction, but weaker global demand and synthetic competition challenge fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: DE BEERS RELATIONSHIP
frictionVectors.details: The state has strengthened its share of diamond value, yet continued dependence on De Beers expertise, marketing, and distribution limits full strategic autonomy.

highlights: Sovereignty rhetoric targets foreign mining influence
Security determines access to resource zones

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY ALIGNMENT
frictionVectors.details: Closer security cooperation with Russian-linked actors may reduce dependence on Western partners but risks opaque concessions, sanctions exposure, and weakened institutional oversight.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND TERRITORIAL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and industrial gold production is constrained by insurgent violence, smuggling, and contested state access to mining regions.

highlights: Critical minerals under tighter state scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Rare-Earth Governance
frictionVectors.details: Informal gold exports and opaque mineral licensing continue to weaken state capture of value. Foreign buyers and regional trading networks retain leverage over supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi remains dependent on external financing for electricity and transport expansion, leaving infrastructure priorities vulnerable to donor and creditor conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in ports, logistics, and maritime surveillance strengthens connectivity but can create dependence on outside commercial and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism concentration and imported fuel dependence leave the economy exposed to external shocks, despite steady progress in renewable-energy deployment.

highlights: Oil, gas, and timber remain externally contested

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Resource Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and politically connected intermediaries retain strong positions in oil, gas, timber, and mining. Weak transparency limits Cameroon’s ability to convert resource wealth into broad domestic gains.

frictionVectors.title: Separatist Infrastructure Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest regions threatens roads, agricultural corridors, and energy projects. External security and infrastructure partners are increasingly important to maintaining state reach.

highlights: External military backing reshapes state authority

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel, commonly associated with the Africa Corps, remain central to regime protection and influence around mining activity. This arrangement risks diverting gold and diamond value away from transparent national revenue systems.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Weak control over roads and borderlands enables smuggling and limits agricultural and mineral commercialization. Armed groups and neighboring conflicts continue to constrain infrastructure recovery.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal model remains heavily dependent on oil exported through the Cameroon pipeline, giving external operators and transit infrastructure significant leverage over national revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict drives refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border instability. N'Djamena is balancing reduced reliance on former French security structures with pressure to diversify external military relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a major sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' control over surrounding maritime resources and migration routes.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external donors and foreign contractors for ports, energy, and transport infrastructure, constraining autonomous development choices.

highlights: Eastern security crisis undermines state control

frictionVectors.title: Mineral supply-chain competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and coltan assets attract intense competition among Chinese, Western, and regional actors, while weak oversight limits the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-backed armed pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and regional forces continues to threaten territorial control, mining zones, and transport corridors in eastern DRC.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil operators and volatile petroleum revenues continue to shape fiscal policy, limiting diversification and reducing bargaining power over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and public works provide essential connectivity but increase exposure to repayment pressures and foreign influence over infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Energy and cocoa value capture improving

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cocoa value chains
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened producer pricing and domestic processing, but multinational traders and global buyers still capture substantial value from the cocoa sector.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore energy and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: New offshore gas and oil development is attracting major foreign investment, creating opportunities for state revenue while raising oversight and contract-governance risks.

highlights: Strategic bases remain the core asset

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and diplomatic leverage but constrain Djibouti's strategic autonomy and expose it to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port debt and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale port and rail investments, particularly those linked to China, have expanded connectivity while intensifying debt, utilization, and refinancing risks.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and Gulf investment expand fiscal room but constrain policy autonomy around strategic assets and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over GERD operations continues to pose a major threat to Egypt's water security and regional influence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining or volatile hydrocarbon output leaves the state reliant on a narrow revenue base and foreign technical and commercial partners.

frictionVectors.title: China-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large externally built infrastructure projects strengthen connectivity but increase dependence on Chinese finance, contractors, and repayment capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-operated mineral projects provide essential export income while limiting domestic control over technology, capital, and value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic pressure
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline sits amid intensifying Red Sea competition, creating sovereignty risks as outside powers seek ports, access, and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, energy, and labor links with South Africa provide stability but constrain Eswatini's room for independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Governance disputes and demands for reform can affect external investment, aid relationships, and the state's ability to manage strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy standoff
frictionVectors.details: The GERD remains a major sovereignty asset for Ethiopia but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan over filling and operations.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western financing supports infrastructure and reform, while debt pressures and conflict limit Addis Ababa's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: The post-transition government is seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese and iron projects, but foreign operators still control major capital, technology, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: French Economic Footprint
frictionVectors.details: France retains commercial and historical influence, while Libreville is diversifying toward Gulf, Asian, and regional partners to increase bargaining room.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: Weak monitoring capacity and opaque licensing create persistent concerns over foreign exploitation of Gambian waters, reducing local food and revenue security.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, and energy development depends heavily on foreign lenders and contractors, limiting fiscal autonomy and increasing exposure to project delays and debt pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated and often foreign-linked mining damages water systems, weakens state authority, and diverts value from formal public revenues despite stronger enforcement efforts.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-Constrained Resource Policy
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions narrow Accra's policy space, even as the government seeks greater domestic processing and public control across gold, cocoa, and oil.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Iron Corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou rail, port, and mining system is financed and operated through powerful foreign consortia, leaving Guinea dependent on external capital and logistics expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Bargaining Gap
frictionVectors.details: Guinea has expanded state demands and local-content requirements, but foreign firms still dominate production, infrastructure, and export value chains in the bauxite sector.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Cashew Trading
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on raw cashew exports and foreign traders leaves producers exposed to volatile prices while limiting domestic processing and fiscal capture.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Limited maritime enforcement enables foreign fishing pressure, while external actors retain strong influence over port activity and broader logistics networks.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and fiscal leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and major debt-service obligations constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders compete for influence over infrastructure and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Mombasa corridors
frictionVectors.details: Port development and regional transport corridors remain exposed to security risks, local opposition, and competition among foreign investors seeking access to East African trade.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen structural dependence on Pretoria. Dam construction, compensation disputes, and project financing remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and customs vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector relies heavily on external market access and foreign-owned factories. Changes in US trade preferences or South African customs arrangements could rapidly weaken domestic economic control.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining companies dominate capital, logistics, and export channels, limiting Liberia's ability to capture full value from its resources. Renegotiation and enforcement of concession terms remain central sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and transport corridor control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and rail infrastructure is essential for exports but can lock the state into long-term commercial dependencies. Weak regulatory capacity increases risks of revenue leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Competing oil authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and budget flows. Foreign firms and states retain leverage through contracts, market access, and diplomatic backing.

frictionVectors.title: Militia and foreign-force infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Airbases, ports, and oil facilities remain entangled with militia interests and external military support. This fragmentation undermines unified resource governance and raises the risk of renewed production disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects are dominated by foreign capital and exposed to volatile global prices. Fiscal benefits and local processing remain insufficient to offset concerns over environmental damage and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, energy, and external financing
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign lenders and operators for ports, roads, and power infrastructure constrains bargaining autonomy. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional actors is increasing around strategic logistics assets.

highlights: Mining diversification remains a strategic priority

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations are narrowing Malawi's policy space. Fuel, fertilizer, and transport infrastructure remain highly exposed to external financing and import costs.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance
frictionVectors.details: Renewed interest in uranium, rare earths, and niobium could diversify exports, but limited regulatory capacity creates risks of weak local value capture and opaque concessions.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over strategic minerals

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and tighter control over foreign operators, increasing friction with international miners and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Linkage
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security forces provides regime protection but may trade long-term resource access and political leverage for short-term military support.

highlights: Iron ore logistics remain externally dependent

frictionVectors.title: GTA Offshore Gas Partnership
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international operators offers major revenue potential, while cross-border governance and revenue-sharing remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and the SNIM rail-port corridor, limiting domestic value addition despite strong state ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Settlement
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty transition over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to British and United States military interests, creating a direct test of Mauritius's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius remains dependent on global financial, tourism, and shipping networks, while Indian Ocean competition places pressure on its port and maritime-security choices.

highlights: Phosphate and green-industry strategy expands leverage

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of phosphate, fisheries, and renewable-energy assets in Western Sahara continues to generate legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some European actors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and United States investment accelerates ports, rail, renewables, and green-hydrogen development, but also creates competing external influence over critical corridors.

highlights: Cabo Delgado insurgency still shadows LNG
Rwanda-backed security enables cautious project revival

frictionVectors.title: LNG Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique retains formal ownership of major gas reserves but depends heavily on foreign operators, financing, and security support to monetize them. Delays and renegotiations continue to limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks and displacement threaten northern communities and constrain energy infrastructure. Rwanda and regional forces improve security around key areas but deepen reliance on external protection.

highlights: Local-content pressure rises with foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries could transform state revenues, but international majors and external investors control much of the capital and technical capacity. Windfall-management and local-benefit rules remain central sovereignty tests.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large projects rely on European and other foreign financing, technology, and export markets. Namibia is seeking stronger domestic participation while avoiding infrastructure becoming externally directed.

highlights: Junta rejects Western security and commercial leverage
Oil transit and uranium access remain contested

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Benin-linked export corridor remains vulnerable to political rupture, sanctions, and operational disruption. Niger seeks greater control over hydrocarbons while lacking the financing and infrastructure to replace external partners quickly.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: The retreat of French and other Western forces has increased reliance on Russian-linked security actors. This enhances regime autonomy in the short term but creates new dependency and reputational risks.

highlights: Oil theft and insecurity erode state capture

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is rebuilding oil and gas output but remains dependent on foreign technology, capital, and operators for complex projects. Contract uncertainty and production-sharing disputes limit the state’s ability to maximize sovereign returns.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Grid Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, attacks in the Niger Delta, and weak electricity infrastructure reduce national control over strategic assets. Private security and external technical support fill gaps that public institutions have not resolved.

highlights: State capacity remains strong and centralized
Eastern Congo conflict raises mineral scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces sustained accusations that its security networks facilitate access to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo minerals, allegations Kigali rejects. International scrutiny and possible sanctions threaten trade, investment, and regional legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda projects influence through disciplined security deployments and partnerships, but remains reliant on foreign aid, investment, and export markets. This creates leverage for external actors despite strong domestic administrative control.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe retains formal control over prospective offshore blocks, but limited technical and financial capacity leaves it dependent on foreign operators. Unproven reserves constrain bargaining power and public revenue expectations.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The country relies on external partners for maritime surveillance and Gulf of Guinea security. This protects shipping and fisheries but increases outside influence over its strategic waters.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN ENERGY CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas output offers Senegal greater fiscal leverage, while international firms and lenders retain major roles in financing, technology, and marketing. Contract reviews and local-content demands are testing relations with investors.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND DEBT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure needs and fiscal constraints limit Dakar's room to negotiate with external financiers. Chinese, Gulf, European, and multilateral funding compete for influence around ports, transport, and energy systems.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME ACCESS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from cooperation with India, France, and other partners on maritime security, but its location makes port access and surveillance politically sensitive. Victoria must balance security assistance without surrendering strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND CLIMATE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and climate stress challenge national control over the blue economy. Limited enforcement capacity creates recurring risks of overfishing and unequal value capture.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, gold, and other minerals remain heavily dependent on foreign capital, operators, and export logistics. Government efforts to raise royalties and local benefits face strong investor and commodity-market constraints.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports rely on externally financed roads, rail links, and port infrastructure. These arrangements can improve capacity but risk locking the country into enclave-style projects with limited domestic industrial spillovers.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY ARCHITECTURE
frictionVectors.details: Somalia depends on international and regional forces, bilateral military partners, and donor financing to contain al-Shabaab and build state capacity. This assistance is essential but limits independent control over security priorities and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, FISHERIES, AND MARITIME CLAIMS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, neighboring countries, and other external actors compete for influence around ports, fisheries, and maritime access. Disputes involving federal and regional authorities complicate unified control of coastal resources and offshore agreements.

highlights: Power and rail reforms remain decisive

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-Supply Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Chinese processing and investment ties against Western efforts to secure platinum-group metals, manganese, and other critical minerals. Export controls and beneficiation policy remain tools for preserving domestic value.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and Grid Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Port congestion, rail constraints, and electricity-sector weakness continue to reduce state control over mineral exports and raise dependence on private operators and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Pipeline Exposure
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenue depends on infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, leaving production and fiscal sovereignty exposed to pipeline damage, transit disputes, and competing Sudanese authorities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Oil Economy
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Malaysian, and Indian-linked operators remain central to production and financing, while opaque contracts and elite patronage limit domestic control over reserves and revenues.

highlights: Red Sea access gains strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Gold and External War Finance
frictionVectors.details: Gold extraction and smuggling finance rival armed networks, with outside actors accused of backing different sides and exploiting weak customs and border controls.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, oil-export routes, and agricultural corridors is strategically contested, drawing interest from Gulf states, Egypt, and Russia while the conflict erodes national bargaining power.

highlights: Gas and mining terms are renegotiated

frictionVectors.title: LNG Investment Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Planned offshore gas development brings major international capital and technology but creates pressure over fiscal terms, local content, and the state's ability to retain value from strategic reserves.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Trade Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and other partners are competing for influence around Dar es Salaam and regional rail links, raising concerns about concession terms and long-term control of logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port Dependence and Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a corridor for landlocked Sahelian economies increases the value of foreign-backed port, road, and logistics infrastructure while limiting the state's room to resist commercial and political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and illicit trade moving south from Burkina Faso threaten transport corridors and could increase reliance on external security assistance and intelligence partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: European migration and finance pressure
frictionVectors.details: The EU remains a critical source of trade, budget support, and migration cooperation, giving Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress and limited access to external financing narrow Tunisia's room to negotiate.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and phosphate vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy capacity and disruptions in phosphate production constrain export earnings and increase reliance on imported fuel and external investment.

frictionVectors.title: East African Crude Oil Pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's oil export strategy depends on the Tanzania-linked pipeline and foreign consortium financing, leaving project timelines, market access, and environmental disputes exposed to external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Gulf-linked firms remain prominent in roads, energy, and logistics, improving capacity while increasing Uganda's exposure to creditor, procurement, and long-term concession risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper remains the core of Zambia's export economy, but foreign-owned mines, traders, and processing networks capture much of the value. Lusaka is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and multilateral support have improved fiscal room, but transport corridors, power supply, and mining investment remain vulnerable to creditor and external-financier conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral investment competition
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export controls and beneficiation demands to capture more value from lithium, platinum, gold, and other minerals, but financing and technology gaps keep the sector dependent on foreign investors.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, arrears, and monetary fragility
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, unresolved external arrears, and recurring currency instability restrict access to conventional finance. Zimbabwe increasingly relies on non-Western lenders, commodity-backed arrangements, and informal channels.
